summary:
Nova Scotia stands under the Canadian national framework, which the parent record carries. Within provincial competence, the province operates no restrictive trans-specific legislation and instead maintains an explicit inclusion framework.

The Government of Nova Scotia released the province's first 2SLGBTQIA+ Action Plan on 8 January 2026, developed under the Dismantling Racism and Hate Act passed in 2022, described by the province as the first Canadian law of its kind to explicitly acknowledge 2SLGBTQIA+ people. The plan was informed by more than 600 community members through surveys, virtual meetings and consultations, and maps actions to improve programs and policies supporting full inclusion of 2SLGBTQIA+ people.

On 10 June 2026 the province announced more than $176,000 through the first round of its 2SLGBTQIA+ Community Impact Grant program, including $12,067 to SeaHorse Sexual Health Centre for queer and trans outreach on the Eastern Shore, $25,000 to LakeCity Works' Queer Careers program in Dartmouth, $25,000 to Pictou County Pride, and $50,000 to Truro Pride to host the province's first provincial 2SLGBTQIA+ conference. Per-project grants are capped at $25,000 from the 2025-26 fiscal year.

Discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and accommodation is prohibited in Nova Scotia as in all Canadian provinces, territories and the federal government; as of 2017 all Canadian jurisdictions explicitly include gender identity as a prohibited ground in their human rights acts. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in Nova Scotia under provincial rules.

The documented Nova Scotia correctional case concerns a transgender woman from the Halifax region held in a men's prison while serving a two-year robbery sentence. On 18 March 2025 a federal judge granted her more time to file her application for judicial review of that placement, citing a lack of transparency and clear, timely communication in the institutional decision-making and systemic barriers restricting her access to her lawyer. No later instance of this case is documented in the record.

Statistics Canada reported on 30 March 2026 that 4,882 police-reported hate crimes were recorded nationally in 2024, a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000, down 2% in 2024 and up 142% since 2018; eight provinces recorded stable or declining rates. The release carries no Nova Scotia-specific rate or incident count. The underlying analysis of sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations comes from Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis report.

In the 2024 Spartacus Gay Travel Index, Canada including Nova Scotia shared first place with Malta, New Zealand, Spain and Portugal among 213 countries and regions as a travel destination covering lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex people.
tangentialFactors:
A 2020 poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office found 87.6% of respondents said they would be "comfortable" if a neighbour was a transgender person, while 91.8% said the same of a gay, lesbian or bisexual neighbour. The figure measures comfort with a neighbour, not law, enforcement or protection outcomes, and no Nova Scotia-specific tolerance, enforcement or facility-access data appears in the record.

Other Canadian provinces have moved in a restrictive direction on trans-related matters: Saskatchewan's Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act 2023 requires parental consent for students under 16 using a gender-related preferred name or gender identity, passed invoking the notwithstanding clause; Alberta's 2024 Health Statutes Amendment Act, Education Amendment Act and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act faced legal challenges which the Alberta government sought to block through Bill 9 in 2025, also using the notwithstanding clause. Nova Scotia has enacted no comparable measure.

The Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologised in December 2020 for harm to Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer communities and created an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to identify and eliminate implicit bias and systemic barriers.

No trans-specific violence or killing figure for Nova Scotia appears in the inventory, so no comparison against a general homicide rate can be drawn; the magnitude of any such harm in the province is not sourced here.

The record contains no Nova Scotia-specific data on airport or border screening treatment of trans travellers, document-marker practice at provincial or federal points of entry, or facility-access outcomes; these remain not sourced.
